text:
The surest measure of a poet's worth, in Johnson's judgment, is the length of time through which his works continue to be read. Praise given by contemporaries may spring from friendship or from the novelty of a manner; it proves little, because the causes that produce it pass away with the generation that felt them. A writer who is still read when those causes have vanished must owe his place to something more durable, and Johnson held that no other proof of excellence could be so secure.

By this test Shakespeare had already been tried. A century and a half had gone by since the plays were first acted. The language had altered and the customs of the stage had altered, and the taste of readers had been reformed more than once by critics who found much in him to censure. Yet the plays were still acted and still read, and their hold upon the public had grown rather than weakened. Johnson put the matter in a single figure: "The stream of time, which is continually washing the dissoluble fabricks of other poets, passes without injury by the adamant of Shakespeare." (Johnson 1765)
